title: Owning a Home, Not Just a House
author: We Made People
summary: A pastor and father of ten uses his hobby of collecting childhood comic books -- and the distinction between 'raw' readable copies and sealed, sold-for-profit graded ones -- as an extended analogy for how modern culture treats homes primarily as financial assets rather than as family inheritance. He argues a house's core value is not its resale price but its function as the physical setting of a family's story: where meals are shared, children learn to walk, doorframe height marks accumulate, and in his own case, where one son was born and another is buried on the property. He frames passing a childhood home to the next generation as 'a little baton of history' rather than merely a financial gift, and shares that losing his own grandmother's farm to a sale outside the family in 1997 was devastating to him personally. The essay closes by redefining the wealth he wants to build for his children as 'a wealth of traditions, a wealth of skills, a wealth of memories, the wealth of a place where you belong' rather than purely monetary inheritance.
points: The author uses comic-book collecting (readable 'raw' copies vs. sealed, investment-grade 'slabbed' copies) as an extended analogy for treating homes purely as financial assets rather than as lived family inheritance.
He frames a family home's core value as being the physical setting of a family's story -- doorframe height marks, a child born in the house, a child buried on the property -- not its resale price.
He describes losing his own grandmother's farm to an outside sale in 1997 as personally devastating ('it killed me. I actually cried'), grounding the essay's argument in direct personal loss.

The essay closes by redefining the wealth he wants to build for his children as 'a wealth of traditions, a wealth of skills, a wealth of memories, the wealth of a place where you belong' rather than primarily monetary inheritance.
quotes: What I do think is that a house is, at its core, more than a financial investment. It is your home. It is the place where you share meals together, where kids learn to walk, and, in some cases, where they were even born.

It is something that can be passed down from one generation to the next. When a family member gives another family member the childhood home, it's much more than a financial gift. It's a little baton of history.
My son Pascal is buried on this property. My son Fox was born in this house. This is our home, and I want it to stay in the family. I want it to be part of our roots.
The only childhood home I have is my grandmother's farm, which was sold to a non-family member in 1997. It killed me. I actually cried.
I am very interested in accumulating wealth for my family, but of a robust sort: a wealth of traditions, a wealth of skills, a wealth of memories, the wealth of a place where you belong.
